chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
title: No recordings but regular radio broadcasts
summary: Reason says the band never recorded and discusses the unpaid radio broadcasts in the towns they played.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: all of them at all? No, we didn't record the whole time that I was with him. We had a session to go to New York to record. But he never did have the band that Joe Glazer wanted. The band had changed the style. And this is why Paul Vaughan used to tell me about, if you're going to have a band, try to get seasoned musicians. So your style can be standard. Because you couldn't take a man like King Oliver's style and make a progressive band out of it. And playing with King, unless it was the whole ensemble playing together, when he's playing solo, you had to play soft. Because he didn't believe in the band, he was playing, he was strained. And we didn't have mics. And you could hear him. But he'd be pierced through a crowd of people, just like the clarinet or cymbal do. And you could hear every bit of it. So, we didn't get the band. And we didn't get the rank out of a band. Because all his recording was done in the 20s. Well, what about broadcasting on the radio? Oh yeah, we used to broadcast plenty. See, we were in Nashville, Tennessee, at Ridgeway Inn. And then almost all the big places that we played, we were in Nashville, Tennessee, at Ridgeway Inn. And then almost all the big places that we played, we broadcast. And in Huntington, West Virginia, we stayed there a whole winter. And we headquartered there. And we broadcast from there, from the studio, every week. But we don't have any recordings of them.

Did you ever broadcast on WSAZ? Where was that? I think that was in Huntington. Probably that, probably so. I don't remember the call. You don't remember the call. That was like W-M-M-N. That's in Fairmont, West Virginia.

No, but we broadcast all the other places that we played at. We broadcast. We always had to get in early enough so we could go to the studio. They didn't have that hookup in the dance hall or something like they have now.
That's interesting that you broadcast in all these different places. Oh, yeah. To me, I just, you know, all these different jobs you played and stuff. Now you have to get there early.

Yeah, yeah, before, early enough to broadcast that evening and then go back and get set up over again to play the dance. And all those different towns, did they pay you for broadcasting? No, not in those days.
That was like advertisement. Yeah. I see. If King got paid, we don't know anything about it.
